abstract: The size and complexity of the human cerebral cortex results from precisely coordinated neural progenitor expansion, differentiation, and fate trajectories for which the controlling molecular programs are not well understood. Pathogenic missense and deletion variants in the protein kinase TAOK1 cause a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability and macrocephaly. We generated human cortical organoids harboring catalytically-inactive TAOK1 disease variant and utilized quantitative phosphoproteomics along with single-cell transcriptomics to uncover disease mechanisms. Catalytically-inactive TAOK1 increases neural progenitor proliferation, accelerates cortical organoid growth, and alters the diversity of cortical cell-types. Phosphoproteomic analyses revealed impaired Hippo signaling with reduced inhibitory phosphorylation of YAP1 concomitant with its sustained nuclear accumulation and activation of TEAD dependent transcription. Progenitors derived from a patient with heterozygous TAOK1 deletion also accumulate nuclear YAP1, extending this finding to a distinct clinical disease-associated TAOK1 lesion. Single-cell transcriptomics demonstrate premature emergence of astrocytic and inhibitory neuronal populations in mutant organoids. Pharmacological inhibition of YAP-TEAD signaling reduced cyclin-A2 labeling and suppressed perturbed Hippo pathway targets. These findings identify TAOK1 as a molecular brake on human cortical overgrowth, implicate previously unrecognized role for Hippo dysfunction in macrocephaly, and reveal pathogenic consequences of accelerated progenitor cycling for both progenitor expansion and fate.
